source: Wu et al. (2022) Autoformalization with Large Language Models
finding: Founding LLM study. Few-shot prompted Codex and PaLM translate competition math statements into Isabelle. The authors estimate the models saw very little Isabelle in training (under 0.18% of Codex data).
numbers: Human check of 150 random MATH problems (50 algebra, 50 number theory, 50 intermediate algebra): Codex translated 38 perfectly = 25.3%.
quote: LLMs can correctly translate a significant portion (25.3%) of mathematical competition problems
limits: One model, greedy decoding, one human judgement per item. Most failures were misaligned informal and formal definitions (for example 'greatest possible value' not mapped to Max).
agent_relevance: Baseline: even a strong model gets about 1 in 4 statements fully right. Formal output needs a separate check, not trust.

source: Wu et al. (2022) Autoformalization with Large Language Models (BLEU and scale)
finding: Scale and code pretraining both help. BLEU against human Isabelle on miniF2F rises from PaLM 8B to 540B, and Codex beats PaLM 540B.
numbers: BLEU algebra / number theory: PaLM 8B 31.49/22.10; 64B 43.13/31.43; 540B 50.30/36.16; Codex 57.13/43.33. 10 prompt problems per subject; 130 algebra and 110 number theory for test.
limits: BLEU measures surface match, not meaning. Later work shows it is a weak proxy (see a13, a14).
agent_relevance: Pick a code-heavy model as translator. Do not use BLEU as a correctness signal.

source: Wu et al. (2022) Autoformalization with Large Language Models (case studies)
finding: In-context examples matter a lot. Codex invented a non-existent Isabelle name ('linear f') for a 'linear function' until the prompt held one example that defines a line, then it formalized it perfectly. The authors searched the web for the outputs and found no sign of memorisation.
numbers: Case study 3: wrong without the example, perfect after one tangential example.
limits: Memorisation test was web search of the first result page only. Case studies are hand-picked.
agent_relevance: Put the missing definition into the context. Retrieval of relevant definitions is part of the job (see a10, a24).

source: Wu et al. (2022) Autoformalization with Large Language Models (expert iteration on autoformalized theorems)
finding: Autoformalized statements were used as training data for a neural prover. Codex formalized 3908 MATH statements, 3363 were syntactically correct, the prover proved some, and training on those proofs raised miniF2F scores.
numbers: Proofs found: iteration 1 = 782 of 3363 (23.3%); iteration 2 = 1011 (30.1%). miniF2F valid/test: base 28.3/29.9; after iter 1 36.1/34.0; after iter 2 37.3/35.2 (5.6 points above prior best).
limits: Statements may be wrong yet provable. The gain is from data volume, not proof that statements are faithful.
agent_relevance: A proved but unfaithful statement is worthless. A faithfulness check must come before trusting a proof.

source: Wu et al. (2022) Autoformalization with Large Language Models (informalization)
finding: The reverse direction, formal to informal, is far easier. Of 38 expert-picked Isabelle items, 36 gave a coherent statement.
numbers: 29 of 38 (76%) more-or-less correct, versus 25% for formalization.
quote: for advanced mathematics, the model is better at informalization than formalization
limits: Small hand-picked set of 38. 'More-or-less correct' is lenient.
agent_relevance: Back-translation is cheap and can act as a consistency check (see a20).

source: Jiang et al. (2022) Draft, Sketch, and Prove
finding: Autoformalization of PROOFS as sketches. A model drafts an informal proof, maps it to a formal sketch with open gaps, and an automated prover (Sledgehammer) fills the gaps.
numbers: miniF2F valid/test: Sledgehammer 9.9/10.4; with heuristics 18.0/20.9; Thor 28.3/29.9; Thor plus expert iteration 37.3/35.2; DSP with human informal proofs 42.6/39.3; with Minerva 62B proofs 43.9/37.7; Minerva 540B 42.6/38.9. 200 of 488 problems proved.
limits: Test gain over Thor plus expert iteration is only a few points. Isabelle only.
agent_relevance: Split into draft, formalize, then verify with a tool. Mirrors plan then check.

source: Jiang et al. (2022) Draft, Sketch, and Prove (ablations)
finding: Each part of the pipeline pays. Removing in-line informal comments, removing the informal draft, or removing the prover each lowers success.
numbers: Valid/test drops: no in-line comments -4.9/-2.8; no informal proofs -3.7/-5.3; no automated prover (model writes full proofs) -9.8/-9.0.
limits: Drops are small and single run, no confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: The external checker or prover is the biggest single contributor. Keep a hard verifier in the loop.

source: Jiang et al. (2022) Draft, Sketch, and Prove (wrong informal proofs)
finding: Flawed informal proofs can still yield valid formal proofs. In a manual check of 50 Minerva proofs that were formalized successfully, only 58% were correct.
numbers: 29 of 50 correct; 16 had an identifiable wrong step; 5 were nonsensical restatements of the goal. So 21 wrong drafts still led to formal proofs.
limits: Sample of 50. Shows draft quality is no guarantee of validity and also that a prover can repair drafts.
agent_relevance: Informal reasoning is a hint, not ground truth. The verifier decides.

source: Azerbayev et al. (2023) ProofNet
finding: ProofNet gives 371 undergraduate-level problems in Lean 3, each with a formal statement, an informal statement and an informal proof. It is much harder than contest benchmarks. Correctness was judged by human experts.
numbers: Few-shot Codex (code-davinci-002) formalizes 13.4% correctly; typecheck 23.7%, BLEU 25.1. proofGPT-1.3B and 6.7B: 0%.
limits: Human-judged on one benchmark. Later work found many ProofNet entries were themselves wrong (see a14).
agent_relevance: Textbook-level content is where the gap is. Expect low base accuracy outside contest math.

source: Azerbayev et al. (2023) ProofNet (retrieval and backtranslation)
finding: Two methods raise accuracy. Prompt retrieval: draft a formalization, embed it, fetch 4 nearest Mathlib statements (90,530 in the base) and add them to the prompt. Distilled backtranslation: Codex writes informal text for Mathlib theorems and a small student is fine-tuned on the pairs.
numbers: Prompt retrieval with Codex: typecheck 45.2%, accuracy 16.1% (up from 13.4%). Distilled backtranslation proofGPT-1.3B: typecheck 19.4%, accuracy 3.2% (up from 0%). Informalization by Codex: 62.3% accuracy, 100% compile.
limits: Gains modest (13.4 to 16.1). Retrieval keyed on the draft output beat keying on the input in preliminary tests; no numbers given. Table cells were read from garbled text extraction.
agent_relevance: Retrieve by the DRAFT output, not the question. Typecheck rate rises far more than true accuracy, a warning sign.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Multilingual Mathematical Autoformalization (MMA)
finding: MMA is a dataset built by informalizing formal statements with GPT-4: 244,238 pairs from Isabelle AFP and 88,536 from Lean 4 mathlib4. Fine-tuning LLaMA 33B on it makes autoformalization work. Joint training on both languages beats single-language training.
numbers: 100 problems (50 miniF2F, 50 ProofNet) judged by two blind experts on a 0-4 effort scale. Base LLaMA 33B: 0% compile. Isabelle-only model compiles 36% / 30%; joint model 24% / 18%. Acceptable with no or minor correction: joint model 16% (Isabelle) and 18% (Lean 4); single-language models 6-11%. Lean 4 compile miniF2F/ProofNet: Lean-only 14%/6%, joint 20%/4%.
limits: Only 100 problems. Isabelle compile counts are inflated because untyped variables still pass. Joint model saw fewer tokens per language yet scored higher.
agent_relevance: Judge by effort to repair, not only right or wrong. Cross-language transfer exists, so more formal data from any system helps.

source: Lu et al. (2024) Process-Driven Autoformalization in Lean 4 (FormL4)
finding: FormL4 is a large Lean 4 autoformalization dataset (statements and proofs). Process-Driven Autoformalization (PDA) uses Lean compiler feedback to train verifier models and to filter training data. Off-the-shelf models almost always fail.
numbers: Greedy compile rates, Random/Basic/Real test: GPT-4o 1.38/1.53/5.85; GPT-4-Turbo 0.52/1.51/5.35; GPT-3.5 0.43/0.31/5.23; open 7B-34B models 0.02-1.21 (Real up to 1.13). Fine-tuned baseline 21.89/28.76/23.72; RFT 26.21/34.12/26.14; RFT plus verifier-enhanced 27.43/35.67/26.87. Human score Fleiss kappa 0.48; human score on Real test 0.30 versus about 0.73-0.85 on other splits.
limits: Compile rate is not semantic correctness. The Real test is much harder for human-judged fidelity.
agent_relevance: Lean 4 is a moving target and base models fail. A compiler signal helps but does not prove meaning is preserved.

source: Lu et al. (2024) FormalAlign: Automated Alignment Evaluation for Autoformalization
finding: A fine-tuned 7B Mistral model scores whether a formal statement matches its informal text. Each positive pair is augmented with 21 misaligned variants made by five strategies.
numbers: Alignment-Selection score, FormalAlign vs GPT-4: FormL4-Basic 99.21 vs 88.91; FormL4-Random 85.85 vs 90.52; MiniF2F-Valid 66.39 vs 64.34; MiniF2F-Test 64.61 vs 68.31. On an 80-item sample: GPT-4o judge 47.50%, FormalAlign 65.00%, human experts average 79.58% (83.75, 77.50, 77.50), Fleiss kappa 0.49. Experts took about 3 hours per 80 items, the model under 2 minutes.
limits: Mixed: loses to GPT-4 on two sets. Misalignment negatives are synthetic. Human agreement is only moderate (kappa 0.49).
agent_relevance: Even trained experts disagree on fidelity. LLM-as-judge for fidelity is weak (47.5%). Needs a separate, independent check.

source: Poiroux et al. (2024/2025) Reliable Evaluation and Benchmarks for Statement Autoformalization
finding: Introduces BEq+, a symbolic equivalence metric (prove each statement from the other with Lean tactics), plus ProofNetVerif (3,752 human-labelled pairs), ProofNet# (corrected ProofNet) and RLM25 (619 research-level pairs from 6 Lean blueprint projects).
numbers: BEq+ on ProofNetVerif: precision 98.0, recall 48.3, F1 64.7 (BEqL: 100.0 / 30.9 / 47.2). 1,142 of 3,752 pairs are equivalent. Benchmark-level correlation with human accuracy over 65 model/method points: BEq+ Pearson 0.974, Kendall 0.872; BEqL 0.966/0.846; type-check only 0.655/0.560. 31.8% of Lean 4 ProofNet entries had formalization errors.
limits: BEq+ misses over half of true equivalences (recall 48.3). It is conservative, so it underestimates accuracy.
agent_relevance: A strong reference-based check exists for math. Type-check pass rate alone is a poor proxy for truth.

source: Poiroux et al. (2024/2025) Reliable Evaluation and Benchmarks for Statement Autoformalization (test-time compute)
finding: Sampling many candidates, dropping ones that fail type-check, then picking by Self-BLEU or majority vote raises accuracy a lot. Type-check filtering is the critical step. Symbolic-equivalence selection did not beat simpler Self-BLEU or voting.
numbers: GPT-4o on ProofNet#: 31.0% single sample to 45.1% with 50 samples plus selection. Llemma 7B BEq+ pass@n: 4.11% at n=1 to 40.54% at n=1000.
limits: The pass@n ceiling is far above selected accuracy, so selection is the bottleneck.
agent_relevance: Generate several, filter by a hard check, then choose. Same shape as best-of-N with a verifier.

source: Poiroux et al. (2024/2025) Reliable Evaluation and Benchmarks for Statement Autoformalization (research-level, RLM25)
finding: With only the informal statement as input and no file context, models fail on research-level math.
numbers: RLM25 BEq+ (no context): Llama3 8B 12-shot 0.40; Llemma 7B MMA 1.13; Llemma 34B 12-shot 0.79; GPT-4o 12-shot 1.50 (type-check 10.55). A Lean Workbook model reached 23.06% type-check only.
limits: Project context (definitions from the same file) was not supplied, so this is partly a missing-context failure. Table cells partly garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Real use needs the surrounding definitions and file. Context supply is a first-class step.

source: Ying et al. (2024) Lean Workbook
finding: Active-learning loop: autoformalize contest forum problems into Lean 4, check by compile, check by back-translation plus a natural-language inference judge, send failures to humans, retrain. Six rounds.
numbers: 1,088,678 forum questions, 327,870 selected; 205,079 compiled; 57,231 also passed the NLI test. Manual check of tagged samples: 93.5% accuracy on a random sample; stop at about 95% correct. 341 problems added by humans. InternLM-Math-Plus solved 4,898 with 1024 samples (Pass@1024 = 8.6%).
limits: Accuracy comes from small sampled checks (5-10 per tag), not all 57K. The NLI judge is itself a model.
agent_relevance: A three-stage filter (compile, back-translate and compare, human spot check) gives high precision at the cost of recall: only 28% of compiled items survive.

source: Li et al. (2025) Goedel-Prover
finding: Large-scale statement autoformalization feeding a prover. Two formalizers (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B based) turned Numina and AOPS problems into Lean 4. Quality gate: a compile test (CC) and an LLM-judged Faithfulness and Completeness test (FC, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct).
numbers: 1.64M formal statements (1.78M with Lean Workbook). Of 928K informal statements, 760K had two valid formalizations and 123K one. Ablation miniF2F / ProofNet / NuminaTest / average: formalizer A only 56.5/13.8/59.6/43.3; B only 56.2/15.2/60.0/43.8; both 57.6/15.2/61.2/44.7. SFT prover reaches 57.6% Pass@32 on miniF2F.
limits: Two formalizers add about 1 point. The FC judge is a model and no human agreement is reported in the text read.
agent_relevance: Style diversity in formalization helps a little. Data scale comes from autoformalization, not from correctness guarantees.

source: Murphy et al. (2024) Autoformalizing Euclidean Geometry (LeanEuclid)
finding: Neuro-symbolic approach: a theorem prover fills in diagram-only facts, and the LLM only formalizes the stated steps. An SMT-based tool (E3) checks logical equivalence to ground truth automatically.
numbers: Statement accuracy by E3 (5-shot): GPT-4 18.9%, GPT-4V 21.0%; 0-shot about 3.0% and 2.3%. Proofs: GPT-4 18.8%, GPT-4V 23.1% fully correct; median similarity of repaired proofs 61.7% (GPT-4), 64.0% (GPT-4V). Checker false-negative rate estimated 15.8% (3 of 19 unproved items in a sample of 86 were truly equivalent); no false positives found.
limits: Narrow domain: 43 Elements proofs plus 100 UniGeo proofs. Formal system E is a proof system, not a spec language, which hurt statements.
agent_relevance: Where a domain allows automatic equivalence, evaluation can be automatic. Diagram gaps are a general implicit-knowledge problem.

source: Li et al. (2024) Autoformalize Mathematical Statements by Symbolic Equivalence and Semantic Consistency
finding: Pass@1 is far below pass@k for autoformalization. Two self-consistency scores pick the best of k: symbolic equivalence (candidates provably equal to each other cluster) and semantic consistency (informalize the candidate, compare its embedding to the source).
numbers: GPT-4 pass@1 to pass@10 gap of 19.5 to 26.5 points on MATH and miniF2F. SymEq best 1@k: Codex 46.1% on MATH, GPT-4 41.1% on miniF2F. SemCo adds 0.8 to 3.9 points 1@k on MATH. Combined relative gains 0.22-1.35x. DeepSeek-v2 1@k gain +5.1 and +0.8.
limits: SemCo is weaker than SymEq in most cases. Needs provers for equivalence. Isabelle only.
agent_relevance: Agreement across independent samples is a useful fidelity signal, and round-trip informalization is a cheap second signal.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Don't Trust: Verify (DTV)
finding: Use autoformalization to check an LLM's own math answers: formalize problem and solution in Isabelle, prove with automated tools, reject solutions that fail. Two filters detect unfaithful formalizations (vacuous statements, self-critique).
numbers: Solve rate GSM8K / Number theory / Algebra / Prealgebra / MultiArith / average. Single sample Minerva 62B 48.6/12.2/33.3/34.1/85.7/42.8; majority vote Minerva 62B 67.2/23.7/60.8/59.2/96.6/61.5; DTV with Minerva formalization 71.4/31.9/61.8/61.0/98.8/65.0; DTV with GPT-3.5 formalization 79.4/36.1/63.2/63.4/99.0/68.2. Abstract: beats majority voting by more than 12% on GSM8K. Ablation on Number theory (full 31.9): no solution sketch 29.2, no vacuous filter 30.7, no self-critique 30.0.
limits: Row labels were interleaved in the text extraction; I matched rows by the ablation table, where the full DTV Minerva row equals 31.9/61.8/61.0. The 12-point GSM8K gain over majority voting is the GPT-3.5-formalization row (79.4 vs 67.2).
agent_relevance: Autoformalize the problem and the answer, then verify. Vacuity and critique filters guard against formalizing the wrong thing.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM
finding: Autoformalization beyond mathematics: the LLM translates a logic problem into a solver language, a symbolic solver reasons, and solver error messages drive self-refinement.
numbers: Average gain +39.2% over standard prompting and +18.4% over chain of thought (GPT-3.5). Executable-formulation rate before to after self-refinement (GPT-3.5 / GPT-4): ProofWriter 87.3 to 95.6 / 99.0 to 99.0; FOLIO 66.7 to 84.3 / 79.9 to 85.8; AR-LSAT 11.3 to 21.8 / 32.6 to 39.8. CoT gains over standard: FOLIO +11.75, LogicalDeduction +9.41, AR-LSAT -3.2, versus +51.59 ProntoQA and +33.82 ProofWriter.
limits: Executable is not correct. AR-LSAT is mostly unparseable for GPT-3.5 (11.3% executable).
agent_relevance: Translate to a solver and let it reason. Solver errors are clean feedback for repair.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC
finding: LLM as semantic parser into first-order logic with Prover9 doing the deduction. Mixed results: big gains on synthetic ProofWriter, no gain for GPT-4 on FOLIO. Translation is lossy.
numbers: ProofWriter (balanced subset) with LINC: GPT-3.5 96.4%, GPT-4 98.3%; near-perfect at every proof depth. GPT-4 FOLIO: LINC below CoT but McNemar p = 0.58, not significant. StarCoder+ with LINC beats GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 CoT by 38 and 10 points on ProofWriter. LINC predicts Uncertain 57% vs 41% for CoT; mistake overlap between LINC and others 0.14-0.22, versus 0.52-0.56 among in-context methods.
limits: Lost information in FOL translation makes LINC over-predict Uncertain. Synthetic ProofWriter is easy to formalize.
agent_relevance: Neurosymbolic errors differ from CoT errors, so they can be combined. Watch lossy translation.

source: Zhang, Valentino, Freitas (2025) Autoformalization in the Wild: Real-World Definitions
finding: Definitions from Wikipedia (Def_Wiki) and arXiv papers (Def_ArXiv) are harder than miniF2F. Self-correction with only a pass/fail signal is weak. Detailed proof-assistant errors and grounding on library definitions help.
numbers: GPT-4o: success rate 13.78 points lower and first-error position 31.90 points earlier than on miniF2F-Test, on average. DeepSeekMath-7B matches GPT-4o in success rate. Binary-feedback refinement helps GPT-4o but hurts DeepSeekMath-7B and fails for Llama3-8B. Structured refinement gains up to 16% in self-correction; definition grounding cuts undefined-name errors by up to 43%.
limits: Isabelle only. Success means syntactic correctness, not meaning.
agent_relevance: Give the repair step rich error text and the right library context, not just pass/fail.

source: Gao et al. (2024) Herald: A Natural Language Annotated Lean 4 Dataset
finding: Herald translates Mathlib4 into natural language with tactic and informal augmentation, then trains a translator that formalizes statements. Numbers in the paper disagree between abstract and body.
numbers: Abstract: 93.2% Pass@128 on miniF2F-test and 22.5% on a graduate textbook set (vs InternLM2-Math-Plus-7B 74.0 and 7.5; TheoremLlama 50.1 and 4.0). Body: 96.7% on miniF2F-test, 96.3% valid, 23.5% Extract Theorem, 16.0% College COT. Data-mix ablation: ProofNet-valid 50.0% (formal-only pairs) up to 81.6%; 1:1:1 mix 68.3%.
limits: Abstract and body differ (93.2 vs 96.7; 22.5 vs 23.5), so treat as approximate. Judging is model-based and may be lenient. miniF2F may be contaminated.
agent_relevance: miniF2F near 97% but graduate level about 23%: contest benchmarks overstate real ability.

source: Peng et al. (2025) CriticLean
finding: A critic model that checks whether a Lean 4 formalization keeps the meaning is trained and used as a reward and a filter. Compile feedback alone fixes syntax but not logic.
numbers: Human-judged accuracy of Kimina-Autoformalizer-7B: single pass 38.0%; compiler feedback loop 54.0%; compile plus CriticLeanGPT loop 84.0%. On 500 problems, 52.8% succeed with a 200-attempt budget: 12.6% on the first try, plus 40.2% recovered by retries. Corpus FineLeanCorpus has over 285K problems.
quote: While compiler feedback resolves syntactical errors, it fails to detect logical flaws.
limits: Small samples (50 for the table, 500 for the pipeline). Critic and generator are from one group.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that a separate critic step lifts faithfulness well above compile-only checking.

source: Wang, Kaliszyk, Urban (2018) First experiments with neural translation of informal to formal mathematics
finding: Earliest neural machine translation experiments from LaTeX math to Mizar-style formal text. Cited by Wu 2022 and Jiang 2023 as the start of learned autoformalization (seen only as a citation in opened papers).
numbers: Not read this session; no figures recorded.
limits: Recalled from citations only; verify before use.
agent_relevance: Autoformalization as translation is old; the new element is in-context learning with large models.

source: Szegedy (2020) A promising path towards autoformalization and general artificial intelligence
finding: Position paper arguing autoformalization could unlock self-improving reasoning systems. Cited as the framing by Wu 2022, Lu 2024 and others (seen only as a citation).
numbers: Not read this session.
limits: Opinion paper; recalled from citations only.
agent_relevance: Framing: faithful formalization is the gateway to verifiable reasoning.

source: Weng et al. (2025) Autoformalization in the Era of Large Language Models: A Survey
finding: Survey covering the full workflow from data to model to evaluation. Notes that AlphaProof's silver-medal IMO result motivates the field and that proof assistants stay labour-intensive even for experts.
numbers: Only the abstract and introduction were read; no table figures recorded.
limits: Partially read.
agent_relevance: Use as a map of the field; follow its references for items not covered here.
